                                                                                                        ENG513...…….
                                                     Lecture: 21

Content-Based Instruction

It is the teaching of content or information in the language being learned with little or no direct effort to teach the
language separately from the content being taught.

Principles of Content-Based Instruction

    1. Content-Based Instruction better reflects learners' needs for learning a second language
    2. People learn a second language more successfully when they use the language as a means of acquiring
       information, rather than mastering the language for its own sake.

Assumptions of Content-Based Instruction

    1. Language is purposeful
       Role of language as a vehicle for learning content entails the centrality of linguistic entities longer than single
       sentences, because the focus of teaching is how meanings are constructed and communicated through texts and
       discourse.
    2. Language is text and discourse-based
       In a content-based class, students are often involved in activities that link the skills. Hence, students might read
       and take notes, listen and write a summary, or respond orally.
    3. Language use draws on integrated skills
       Language is used for specific purposes. The purpose may be academic, vocational, social, or recreational but
       it gives direction, shape, and ultimately meaning to discourse and texts
    4. Students learn best when instruction addresses students' needs
    5. Teaching builds on the previous experience of the learners

Student goals of an immersion program include
(1) Developing a high level of proficiency in the FL

(2) Developing positive attitudes toward foreign language speakers and their culture(s)

(3) Developing English language skills commensurate with expectations for a student's age and abilities

(4) Gaining designated skills and knowledge in the content areas of the curriculum

Immigrant On-Arrival Programs - focus on the newly arrived immigrants in a country and their need for survival.
Such learners typically need to learn how to deal with differing kinds of real-world content as a basis for social survival.

Students with Limited English Proficiency (SLEP) programs – these are governmentally mandated programs to serve
especially those children whose parents might be served by the on-arrival programs, but more generally designed to
provide in-class instruction to those whose language competence is insufficient to participate fully in normal school
instruction.

Language for Specific Purposes (LSP) - a movement that seeks to serve the language needs of learners who need
language in order to carry out specific roles (e.g., student, engineer, technician, and nurse) rather than master the
language for its own sake.

LSP/EST subfields

       ESP (English for Specific Purposes)
       EOP (English for Occupational Purposes)
       EAP (English for Academic Purposes)

                                                                                                           2
                                                                                                 ENG513...…….
Types of Learning and Teaching Activities: CBI

      Building Language skills
      Building Vocabulary
      Discourse organization
      Communicative interaction
      Synthesis of content materials and grammar
Skills for any CBI instructor

      Varying the format of classroom instruction
      Using group work techniques
      Using process approaches to writing
      Using appropriate error correction techniques
      Maintaining high levels of student esteem

                                                     Lecture: 22

Assumptions of Task-based instruction

      The focus is on process rather than product.
      Learners learn language by interacting communicatively and purposefully
      Basic elements are purposeful activities and tasks
      Activities and tasks of a task-based syllabus are sequenced according to difficulty
      Activities and tasks can be either: those that learners might need to achieve in real life; those that have a
       pedagogical purpose specific to the classroom

Difficulty of a task depends on a range of factors

      Previous experience
      Complexity of the task
      Language required
      The degree of support available

Task-based training identified several key areas of concern

      Analysis of real-world task-use situations
      The translation of these into teaching tasks descriptions
      The detailed design of instructional tasks
      The sequencing of instructional tasks in classroom training

Four major categories of team performance function

   1. Orientation functions (processes for generating and distributing information necessary to task accomplishment
      to team members)
   2. Organizational functions (processes necessary for members to coordinate actions necessary for task
      performance)
   3. Adaptation functions (processes occurring as team members adapt their performance to each other to complete
      the task).
   4. Motivational functions (defining team objectives and "energizing the group" to complete the task)

                                                                                                             3
                                                                                                   ENG513...…….
Academic tasks are defined as having four important dimensions

        The products students are asked to produce
        The operations they are required to use in order to produce these products
        The cognitive operations required
        The accountability system involved

Task types in TBLT

    1.   Diagrams and formations
    2.   Drawing
    3.   Clock faces
    4.   Monthly calendar
    5.   Maps -

ENG(513-518) Glossary

    Accredited :Accredited is (Of a person, organization, or course of study) officially recognized or
     authorized.
    Allocation :The action or process of allocating or sharing out something is called allocation.
    Alternative 'Concurrent' Model :A student simultaneously studies both one or more academic
     subjects, and the ways of teaching that subject, leading to a combined bachelor's degree and
     teaching credential to qualify as a teacher of that subject.
    Anomaly :Something that deviates from what is standard, normal, or expected
    Approach :It is a way of looking at teaching and learning. Underlying any language teaching
     approach is a theoretical view of what language is, and of how it can be learnt. An approach
     gives rise to methods, the way of teaching something, which use classroom activities or
     techniques to help learners learn.
    Assess :Evaluate or judge
    Audio Lingual Method :It is a teaching method and based on behaviorist theory, which
     postulates that certain traits of living things, and in this case humans, could be trained through a
     system of reinforcement. The correct use of a trait would receive positive feedback while
     incorrect use of that trait would receive negative feedback.
    Autonomous :(Of a country or region) having the freedom to govern itself or control its own
     affairs.
    Caution :Vigilance, carefulness
    Collocation :The habitual juxtaposition of a particular word with another word or words with a
     frequency greater than chance is called collocation.
    Communicative Language Teaching Approach :It is an approach to language teaching that
     emphasizes interaction as both the means and the ultimate goal of study.
    Community Language Learning :It is a language-teaching approach in which students work
     together to develop what aspects of a language they would like to learn. It is based on the
     Counselling-approach in which the teacher acts as a counselor and a paraphraser, while the
     learner is seen as a client and collaborator.
    Concocted :Assemble
    Concordance :Agreement or consistency
    Consecutive' Model :A student simultaneously studies both one or more academic subjects, and
     the ways of teaching that subject, leading to a combined bachelor's degree and teaching
     credential to qualify as a teacher of that subject
    Content Based Instruction :The focus of a CBI lesson is on the topic or subject matter. During
     the lesson students are focused on learning about something. This could be anything that
     interests them from a serious science subject to their favourite pop star or even a topical news
     story or film.
    Contextualize :Place or study in context.

Maha Malik’s Compilation                                                                          Page 1

                                 ENG(513-518) Glossary

    Continuous Professional Development :CPD is the process by which teachers (like other
     professionals) reflect upon their competencies, keep them up to date, and develop them
     further.
    Continuum :Range, variety
    Cooperative Language Learning :It is group learning activity organized so that learning is
     dependent on the socially structured exchange of information between learners in groups and
     in which each learner is held accountable for his or her own learning and is motivated to
     increase the learning of others.
    Crucible :A situation of severe trial, or in which different elements interact, leading to the
     creation of something new
    Curricula :It is the plural of curriculum which means syllabus
    Deontology :The study of the nature of duty and obligation
    Dimensions :Aspects, features
    Discourse :In linguistics, discourse refers to a unit of language longer than a single sentence.
     More broadly, discourse is the use of spoken or written language in a social context.
    ESP (English for Specific Purposes) :It stands for English for Specific Purposes. It is defined to
     meet specific needs of the learners. It makes use of underlying methodology and activities of the
     discipline it serves. It is centered on the language appropriate to these activities in terms of
     grammar, lexis, register, study skills, discourse and genre.
    Feedback :Feedback is information given to the learner about his/her performance with the
     objective of improving performance.
    Grammar :Grammar is the set of rules and conventions of language shared by a group of native
     speakers (whereby we decide whether a particular language form is right or wrong).
    Grammar Translation Method :Sometimes also known as the Classical Method, this is a
     traditional teaching technique that was used to teach Latin and Greek and was particularly in
     vogue during the 16th Century. The focus at this time was on the translation of texts, grammar,
     and rote learning of vocabulary. There was no emphasis on speaking and listening
     comprehension because Latin and Greek were taught more as academic subjects rather than a
     means of oral communication.
    In-service :(Of training) intended for those actively engaged in the profession or activity
     concerned.
    Innateness :Existing in, belonging to, or determined by factors present in an individual from
     birth : native
    Interpersonal :The interpersonal function refers to the grammatical choices that enable
     speakers to enact their complex and diverse interpersonal relations. This tenet of systemic
     functional linguistics is based on the claim that a speaker not only talks about something, but is
     always talking to and with others.
    Intrapersonal :It is a communicator's internal use of language or thought. It can be useful to
     envision intrapersonal communication occurring in the mind of the individual in a model which
     contains a sender, receiver, and feedback loop.

1. Which of the following systems deal with the rules of grammar? (syntactic)
2. Hymes has coined an acronym called ____________. (SPEAKING)
3. Stephen Krashen initially studied how children ___________ language and
   later applied it to adults language learning. (learn)
4. Language as a system enables the language user to combine _______ to form
   words, words to form phrases, phrases to form sentences, and sentences to
   form spoken or written texts. (phonemes)
5. SFL stands for ____________________. (systemic functional linguistics)
6. Which of the following methods has been introduced by Lozanov in 1979?
   (Suggestopedia)
7. In a typical Pakistani English classroom, __________ is commonly used.
8. ELT stands for ____________. (English Language Teaching)
9. In the Western world, from 17th to 19th centuries, learning of which of the
   following languages was associated with speaker’s intellectuality? (Greek
   and Latin)
10.      Lack of __________ in the areas of language planning in education is
   the major problem in Pakistan. (research)
11.       In __________, there is no usual listening or speaking practice, and
   very little attention is placed on pronunciation. (GTM)
12.       In a typical Pakistani English classroom, __________ is commonly
   used. (GTM)
13.      GTM failed at the end of the __________ century. (19TH)
14.     Direct Method was established in _____ and Germany around 1900.
   (France)
15.     Audio-lingual Method is basically a/an ___________ Method.
   (American)

16.    One of the important aspects of language teaching/learning is
  ___________. (Culture)
17.     The structural–situational method was developed around 20th century
  in ___________. (Great Britain)
18.     Which of the following is firmly entrenched in the domains of power
  in Pakistan since 1947? (English Language)
19.     The practicality of English language opens innumerable prospects in
  the _____ and financial world. (social)
20.     According to Warsi (1994), ELT methodology in Pakistan is not based
  on _____ approach. (need based)
21.     Richards (2011) identifies the purpose of _____ for curriculum
  development in English language teaching. (needs analysis)
22.     According to Abbas (1998): despite the massive inputs into teaching of
  English, the national results are abysmally _____. (poor)
23.       In Pakistan, the examination system is based on _______________
  skill. (writing)
24.     Reading skill is given importance in _____ education system.
  (Pakistani)
25.     GTM is more commonly used in _____ schools in Pakistan.
  (government)
26.     English has a unique significance around the globe due to its status as
  a _____. (lingua franca)
27.     HE stands for _________. (higher education)
28.     Which of the following methods is derived from the teaching of Greek
  and Latin? (Grammar Translation Method)
29.   The major strength of GTM is to develop the students’ _____.
  (memory)
30.     Which of the following method has been rejected as a legitimate
  language teaching method by modern scholars? (GTM)
31.   The major strength of __________ is to develop the students’ memory.
  (GTM)

32.     Which of the following methods does not have any theory as its
  theoretical framework? (GTM)
33.      The Direct method stresses more on the ability to _____ language rather
  than to analyze it. (use)
34.      The Direct method teaches grammar and _____ through direct
  translations and focuses on the written language. (vocabulary)
35.      In Direct method, both speech and _____ comprehensions are taught.
  (listening)
36.    Which method of foreign language teaching was developed by C. J.
  Dodson? (bilingual)
37.     In the Direct method, understanding of target language becomes easier
  due to the inhibition of the linguistic interferences from the _____. (mother
  tongue)
38.     Which of the following refers to the spread of an item across texts and
  contexts? (range)
39.      Which of the following skills was considered primary by the structural
  linguists? (speech)
40.      The Structural-situational method is centered on which three
  principles? (Selection, gradation and presentation)
41.     Behaviorism was popular in US in _____________. (1920s)
42.      Behaviorists believed that language learning is a process of mechanical
  habit formation through _____. (repetition)
43.      In a Total Physical Response classroom, a teacher plays a/an _____
  role. (active)
44.    Which of the following tradition(s) does the Total Physical Response
  method take inspiration from? (Language teaching procedures,
  Developmental psychology, All of the given options, Humanistic
  pedagogy)
45.     Total Physical Response is a language teaching method built around the
  coordination of _____ and action. (speech)
46.     The analysis regarding a Total Physical Response syllabus reveals the
  use of _____ based program. (sentence)

47.     Total Physical Response method attempts to teach _____ through
  motor activity. (language)
48.     The Silent Way is a language teaching method developed by _____.
  (Caleb Gattegno)
49.     The first part of a Silent Way lesson focuses on _____. (pronunciation)
50.      In the Silent Way method, the teacher focuses on the _____ meaning,
  rather than the communicative value. (propositional)
51.     Silence is the most demanding aspect for _____ of the Silent Way.
  (teachers)
52.     The Silent Way adopts a basic structural syllabus, with lessons planned
  around _____ items and related vocabulary. (grammatical)
53.    A textbook is not considered a necessary component in a Community
  Language Learning classroom because it _____ the growth and interaction.
  (impedes)
54.      A Community Language Learning syllabus emerges from the
  interaction between the learner’s expressed communicative intentions and the
  teacher's reformulations of them into _____ language utterances. (target)
55.    Community Language Learning teachers ought to be familiar with and
  sympathetic to the role of counselors in _____ counseling. (psychological)

                                                                                                        ENG513...…….
                                                     Lecture: 21

Content-Based Instruction

It is the teaching of content or information in the language being learned with little or no direct effort to teach the
language separately from the content being taught.

Principles of Content-Based Instruction

    1. Content-Based Instruction better reflects learners' needs for learning a second language
    2. People learn a second language more successfully when they use the language as a means of acquiring
       information, rather than mastering the language for its own sake.

Assumptions of Content-Based Instruction

    1. Language is purposeful
       Role of language as a vehicle for learning content entails the centrality of linguistic entities longer than single
       sentences, because the focus of teaching is how meanings are constructed and communicated through texts and
       discourse.
    2. Language is text and discourse-based
       In a content-based class, students are often involved in activities that link the skills. Hence, students might read
       and take notes, listen and write a summary, or respond orally.
    3. Language use draws on integrated skills
       Language is used for specific purposes. The purpose may be academic, vocational, social, or recreational but
       it gives direction, shape, and ultimately meaning to discourse and texts
    4. Students learn best when instruction addresses students' needs
    5. Teaching builds on the previous experience of the learners

Student goals of an immersion program include
(1) Developing a high level of proficiency in the FL

(2) Developing positive attitudes toward foreign language speakers and their culture(s)

(3) Developing English language skills commensurate with expectations for a student's age and abilities

(4) Gaining designated skills and knowledge in the content areas of the curriculum

Immigrant On-Arrival Programs - focus on the newly arrived immigrants in a country and their need for survival.
Such learners typically need to learn how to deal with differing kinds of real-world content as a basis for social survival.

Students with Limited English Proficiency (SLEP) programs – these are governmentally mandated programs to serve
especially those children whose parents might be served by the on-arrival programs, but more generally designed to
provide in-class instruction to those whose language competence is insufficient to participate fully in normal school
instruction.

Language for Specific Purposes (LSP) - a movement that seeks to serve the language needs of learners who need
language in order to carry out specific roles (e.g., student, engineer, technician, and nurse) rather than master the
language for its own sake.

LSP/EST subfields

       ESP (English for Specific Purposes)
       EOP (English for Occupational Purposes)
       EAP (English for Academic Purposes)

                                                                                                           2
                                                                                                 ENG513...…….
Types of Learning and Teaching Activities: CBI

      Building Language skills
      Building Vocabulary
      Discourse organization
      Communicative interaction
      Synthesis of content materials and grammar
Skills for any CBI instructor

      Varying the format of classroom instruction
      Using group work techniques
      Using process approaches to writing
      Using appropriate error correction techniques
      Maintaining high levels of student esteem

                                                     Lecture: 22

Assumptions of Task-based instruction

      The focus is on process rather than product.
      Learners learn language by interacting communicatively and purposefully
      Basic elements are purposeful activities and tasks
      Activities and tasks of a task-based syllabus are sequenced according to difficulty
      Activities and tasks can be either: those that learners might need to achieve in real life; those that have a
       pedagogical purpose specific to the classroom

Difficulty of a task depends on a range of factors

      Previous experience
      Complexity of the task
      Language required
      The degree of support available

Task-based training identified several key areas of concern

      Analysis of real-world task-use situations
      The translation of these into teaching tasks descriptions
      The detailed design of instructional tasks
      The sequencing of instructional tasks in classroom training

Four major categories of team performance function

   1. Orientation functions (processes for generating and distributing information necessary to task accomplishment
      to team members)
   2. Organizational functions (processes necessary for members to coordinate actions necessary for task
      performance)
   3. Adaptation functions (processes occurring as team members adapt their performance to each other to complete
      the task).
   4. Motivational functions (defining team objectives and "energizing the group" to complete the task)

                                                                                                             3
                                                                                                   ENG513...…….
Academic tasks are defined as having four important dimensions

        The products students are asked to produce
        The operations they are required to use in order to produce these products
        The cognitive operations required
        The accountability system involved

Task types in TBLT

    1.   Diagrams and formations
    2.   Drawing
    3.   Clock faces
    4.   Monthly calendar

QUESTIONS OF MARKS 3:

Q. Dose digital media support reading materials in L2 classrooms?
Digital media offer a number of ways to enhance materials development
and learner feedback across the traditional skills (for an extended
discussion, see Levy, 2009). Chun (2006) reviewed a number of
technologies available to support reading in a second language, some of
which are available non-commercially such as electronic and online
dictionaries, hyperlinks to vocabulary words that are embedded within
many online texts, or the use of the Internet to obtain a wider range of
sources. She also points towards software that can provide annotations
through multimedia and promote word recognition.
Q. Define self direction with reference to learner autonomy? Self-
direction refers to situations in which learners accept responsibility for
all the decisions concerned with learning but not necessarily for the
implementation of those decisions; Q. How would you define reading?
"Reading" is the process of looking at a series of written symbols and
getting meaning from them. When we read, we use our eyes to receive
written symbols (letters, punctuation marks and spaces) and we use our
brain to convert them into words, sentences and paragraphs that
communicate something to us. Reading can be silent (in our head) or aloud
(so that other people can hear). Reading is a receptive skill - through it we
receive information. But the complex process of reading also requires the
skill of speaking, so that we can pronounce the words that we read. In this
sense, reading is also a productive skill in that we are both receiving

information and transmitting it (even if only to ourselves). Q. How many
types of speaking tasks are there? Give names. There are broadly three
types of speaking tasks that encourage genuine communication among
learners:
communication-gap tasks, discussion tasks, and mono logic tasks Q.
What is the aim of VOLL program?
A VOLL program aims to provide students with an English course
integrated with vocational content.
This vocational content is a starting point for designing English language
programs based on vocational themes, tasks, and language.
Q. Define eclectic approach of language teaching?
Eclectic approach is a method of language education that combines
various approaches and methodologies to teach language depending on the
aims of the lesson and the abilities of the learners.
Q. Repeated viewing in extensive viewing
Repeated viewing leads to repeated encounters with a vocabulary item.
There is no maximum number of times that a learner can watch a given
episode.
Q. Two categories of team performances founded in task based
learning.
1. orientation functions (processes for generating and distributing
information necessary to task accomplishment to team members) 2.
organizational functions (processes necessary for members to coordinate
actions necessary for task performance)
Q. Role of learners as Risk taker and innovator in task based learning
Many tasks will require learners to create and interpret messages for which
they lack full linguistic resources and prior experience. In fact, this is said
to be the point of such tasks. Practice in restating, paraphrasing, using
paralinguistic signals (where appropriate), and so on, will often be needed.
The skills of guessing from linguistic and contextual clues, asking for
clarification, and consulting with other learners may also need to be
developed.
Q. Some context of EIL communication foreign visitor seeking
      information/directions/assistance from
a local resident in a non-English speaking country.
      foreign visitor giving directions to a local taxi driver in a non-
English speaking country          foreign resident seeking and giving
information to a local
official in a non- English speaking country ravellers from different
    countries interacting at an airport/on a
plane/on a train usiness men from different countries negotiating a
contract Q. Underlying assumption behind the synthetic syllabus?

items, or functional categories;

                                          r their understanding and
assimilation.
Q. What is Integrating language skills ?
The primary skills of language identified as listening, speaking, reading,
and writing are connected with one another. We integrate these skills
during every day conversation. It is rarely noted when we only listen, or
only speak, or only read, or only write. It is artificial and tiresome if,we
decide to separate these skills and use only one for a specified period of
time for some peculiar reason,. Such an artificial separation of language
skills is quite normal in most language schools. In North America, and
several other
countries, colleges and universities’ language institutes offer classes based
on isolated skills and proficiency levels with course titles as ‘Beginning
Reading’, ‘Intermediate Listening’, or
‘Advanced Writing’. Curriculum designers and textbook writers have long
been using the separation of skills as a guiding principle for syllabus
construction and materials production. They even try to hardly link a
particular skill with a particular set of learning strategies. They talk about
reading strategies, listening strategies, speaking strategies, and writing
strategies. Oxford (2001, p. 19), has done extensive research on learning
strategies, asserts, “Many strategies, such as paying selective attention,
self-evaluating, asking questions, analyzing, synthesizing, planning and
predicting are applicable across skill areas.”
Q. What are the student’s goals of an immersion program?
(1) Developing a high level of proficiency in the foreign language; (2)
Developing positive attitudes toward those who speak the foreign
language and toward their culture(s);
(3)     Developing English language skills commensurate with
expectations for a student's age and abilities.

Q. Expository Studies
Expository studies focus on explaining or describing phenomena in detail to enhance
understanding. This can include elaborating claims or presenting counter-arguments using
structured discourse.
Q. Vocabulary Learning Rate
L1 learners acquire vocabulary incidentally due to immense input, whereas L2 learners face
limited input and need structured teaching. Teachers significantly influence vocabulary learning
in L2 settings by carefully planning and providing appropriate resources.
Q. Three Strategies for Teaching Pronunciation
   ❖       Phonetic practice: Engaging learners in exercises focusing on sound articulation.
   ❖       Listening discrimination: Using audio materials to identify correct pronunciation.
   ❖       Integration with vocabulary: Combining pronunciation with vocabulary lessons to
           enhance retention.
Q. Teaching and Learning Pronunciation: Three Points
   1.      Stress and intonation are critical for meaning comprehension.
   2.      Learners should focus on naturalistic speech contexts.
   3.      Use of technology, like audio recording, can help practice.
Q. Main Factors on Which Content-Based Instruction Depends
Content-based instruction depends on:
   ❖       Relevance of content to learners’ needs.
   ❖       Integration of language skills with subject matter.
   ❖       Availability of authentic and pedagogically sound materials.
Q. Lexical Variety and Its Significance
Lexical variety ensures richness in language use, impacting reading comprehension and
communication fluency. It involves exposure to diverse vocabulary contexts.
Q. Learner Autonomy
Learner autonomy refers to the ability of learners to take responsibility for their own learning
through self-directed activities, critical reflection, and decision-making.
Q. Techniques to Overcome Communication Barriers and Ensure Clarity
   1.      Using simple and clear language.
   2.      Encouraging active listening.
   3.      Incorporating visual aids.

Q. Metacognitive Strategies
Metacognitive strategies include planning, monitoring, and evaluating one’s learning processes,
particularly effective in enhancing comprehension and self-regulation.
Q. Three Theory-Based Listening Types
   1.      Interactive listening: Listening in real-time conversations.
   2.      Intensive listening: Focused on details and specific inputs.
   3.      Extensive listening: Listening for general understanding and context.
Q. Listening Comprehension
Listening comprehension involves understanding spoken language by identifying main ideas,
details, and implications using various cognitive and linguistic skills.
Q. Characteristics of Listening (as per a specific researcher)
Skehan emphasizes that listening tasks focus on meaning, are interactive, and encourage
comprehension beyond surface-level interpretations.
Q. Define the Term Curriculum
Curriculum refers to the structured plan of educational content, objectives, and methods designed
to achieve specific learning outcomes.
Q. Difference Between Synthetic and Analytic Syllabus
           ❖       Synthetic syllabus focuses on pre-determined language components taught
                   sequentially.
           ❖       Analytic syllabus revolves around tasks or content where learners infer rules
                   through exposure.

A lesson plan serves to organize content, set learning objectives, guide instructional methods, and
evaluate outcomes.
Q. Lesson Plan Approaches Suggested by Different Scholars
Scholars propose integrating pre-task, task, and post-task phases to enhance clarity and learner
engagement.

These assessments are tailored by teachers to match students' needs, focusing on specific learning
goals and feedback mechanisms.
Q. Conference Assessments
These involve one-on-one discussions between teachers and students, focusing on progress,
challenges, and individualized feedback.

commercially such as electronic and online dictionaries, hyperlinks to vocabulary words that are

points towards software that can provide annotations through multimedia and promote word recognition.

        abilities;

ENG513 Final-term Solved Papers
                     By AQ
  Q. Why did the linguists feel the need for integration of language skill for various learners? Briefly
                                           discussed 5 Marks

Theoretical as well as experiential knowledge pointed out the importance of integrating language skills.
The learning and use of any skill can trigger cognitive and communicative associations with the others.
Several scholars have attested this possibility. Emphasizing the connection between reading and other
skills, Krashen (1989, p. 90) argues that reading may very well be “the primary means of developing
reading comprehension, writing style, and more sophisticated vocabulary and grammar.” Similarly,
listening activities have been found to help learners make the broader connection between the
sociolinguistic concept of form and function and the psycholinguistic processes of interpretation and
expression (Rost, 1990). Linking speaking with other skills, Bygate (1998, p. 34) found it inevitable that
the real time processing of listening activities, the exposure to language via reading and listening, and
the attention to form-meaning relations in all skills can wash forward to help the development of
speaking. Such a connection is true of writing as well, observed by Rivers (1981, pp. 296–7). “Writing is
not, then, a skill which can be learned in isolation the most effective writing practice, and the most
generally useful, will have a close connection with what is being practiced in relation to other skills.”

In addition to these theoretical insights, there is another advantage for repeating the natural integration
of skills in the classroom. Various learners bring various learning styles and strategies to the class.
Integration of language skills has the potential to offer different opportunities for different types of
learners, for example, the extroverts who like to speak a lot, the introverts who prefer to listen or read,
and the analytically or visually oriented learners who like to see how words are written and sentences
constructed (Davies & Pearse, 2000, p. 75). Selinker and Tomlin (1986) urge for more classroom-
oriented research is required to determine the full impact of integration and separation of skills, all
available theoretical and experiential information stress the need to integrate language skills for
effective language learning and teaching.

Q. Keeping in view Task-based Language Teaching. Task activity and achievements are motivational? 5
Marks

Yes, Task Activity and Achievement are Motivational.

Tasks are also said to improve learner motivation and therefore promote learning. This is because they
require the learners to use authentic language, they have well-defined dimensions and closure, they are
varied in format and operation, they typically include physical activity, they involve partnership and
collaboration, they may call on the learner's past experience, and they tolerate and encourage a variety

Qayyum.gcu@gmail.com                                                                         03360672982

of communication styles. One teacher trainee, commenting on an experience involving listening tasks,
noted that such tasks are "genuinely authentic, easy to understand because of natural repetition;
students are motivated to listen because they have just done the same task and want to compare how
they did it" (quoted in Willis 1996, pp. 61-62).

Q. What is the aim of VOLL program? 3 Marks

A VOLL program aims to provide students with an English course integrated with vocational content.
This vocational content is a starting point for designing English language programs based on vocational
themes, tasks, and language.

Q. Considered the context of Pakistan enlist the important perspectives for learner autonomy? 5
Marks

The term ‘autonomy’ is derived originally from the fields of politics and moral philosophy and is widely
confused with self-instruction and independent learning (Benson, 2001, 2007). The concept of learner’s
autonomy has first developed in the early 1970’s in France. In educational circles, autonomy is
considered a worthy goal for philosophical as well as for psychological reasons. From a philosophical
point of view, one of the desirable goals of general education has been to make individuals autonomous

  Q. Why did the linguists feel the need for integration of language skill for various learners? Briefly
                                           discussed 5 Marks

Theoretical as well as experiential knowledge pointed out the importance of integrating language skills.
The learning and use of any skill can trigger cognitive and communicative associations with the others.
Several scholars have attested this possibility. Emphasizing the connection between reading and other
skills, Krashen (1989, p. 90) argues that reading may very well be “the primary means of developing
reading comprehension, writing style, and more sophisticated vocabulary and grammar.” Similarly,
listening activities have been found to help learners make the broader connection between the
sociolinguistic concept of form and function and the psycholinguistic processes of interpretation and
expression (Rost, 1990). Linking speaking with other skills, Bygate (1998, p. 34) found it inevitable that
the real time processing of listening activities, the exposure to language via reading and listening, and
the attention to form-meaning relations in all skills can wash forward to help the development of
speaking. Such a connection is true of writing as well, observed by Rivers (1981, pp. 296–7). “Writing is
not, then, a skill which can be learned in isolation the most effective writing practice, and the most
generally useful, will have a close connection with what is being practiced in relation to other skills.”

In addition to these theoretical insights, there is another advantage for repeating the natural integration
of skills in the classroom. Various learners bring various learning styles and strategies to the class.
Integration of language skills has the potential to offer different opportunities for different types of
learners, for example, the extroverts who like to speak a lot, the introverts who prefer to listen or read,
and the analytically or visually oriented learners who like to see how words are written and sentences
constructed (Davies & Pearse, 2000, p. 75). Selinker and Tomlin (1986) urge for more classroom-
oriented research is required to determine the full impact of integration and separation of skills, all
available theoretical and experiential information stress the need to integrate language skills for
effective language learning and teaching.

Answer:
In a remote area of Pakistan, where access to resources may be limited, adopting learner-centered teaching methodologies is crucial for effective English language instruction. Here are some strategies that can be employed:
    1. Interactive Learning Activities:
    • Use interactive activities that encourage students to actively participate in the learning process. For example, group discussions, role-playing, and language games can engage students and promote communication skills.
    • Evidence: Research consistently shows that interactive activities enhance language acquisition by providing real-life contexts for language use and promoting meaningful communication.
    2. Project-Based Learning:
    • Assign projects that require students to apply their language skills in real-world scenarios. This could involve creating presentations, writing articles, or even producing short videos in English.
    • Evidence: Project-based learning not only improves language proficiency but also develops critical thinking, problem-solving, and creativity, as supported by educational research.
    3. Technology Integration:
    • Leverage technology, even in resource-constrained environments. Utilize smartphones, if available, for language learning apps, online resources, and interactive multimedia content.
    • Evidence: Studies indicate that technology integration can enhance language learning by providing additional resources, immediate feedback, and opportunities for self-directed learning.
    4. Differentiated Instruction:
    • Recognize and accommodate diverse learning styles and abilities in the classroom. Tailor teaching methods to address individual needs, allowing students to progress at their own pace.
    • Evidence: Differentiated instruction is supported by educational research, promoting inclusivity and ensuring that each student has the opportunity to succeed.
    5. Cultural Relevance:
    • Integrate local culture and context into English lessons. Incorporate examples, stories, and activities that resonate with the students' daily lives, making the language more relevant and meaningful.
    • Evidence: Research suggests that culturally relevant teaching enhances student engagement and motivation, fostering a positive attitude towards learning.
    6. Formative Assessment:
    • Use ongoing, formative assessments to gauge student progress and adjust teaching strategies accordingly. Provide constructive feedback that guides students towards improvement.
    • Evidence: Formative assessment practices have been shown to enhance learning outcomes by identifying areas for improvement and encouraging a growth mindset.
    7. Teacher as Facilitator:
    • Shift the role of the teacher from a lecturer to a facilitator. Guide and support students in their learning journey, fostering independence and self-directed learning.
    • Evidence: Educational theories such as constructivism emphasize the importance of a facilitative role for teachers, promoting active engagement and deeper understanding.
By implementing these learner-centered approaches, English language instruction in a remote area of Pakistan can become more effective, engaging, and relevant to the students' lives. Adaptability and a focus on the students' needs will contribute to a positive and enriching learning environment.

Benjamin Lee Whorf said, “Language shapes the way we think, and determines what we can
think about.” How would you support this argument?

Language isn’t just a way to communicate, it’s a component of culture that makes it unique and
specific. When language and culture are discussed, the phrase “language is culture and culture is
language” is often mentioned because the two are always intertwined. This means that the language
you speak reflects what your values and beliefs are.

The language you speak reflects what your values and beliefs are.
CLICK TO TWEET

According to anthropological linguist Daniel Everett, language can be considered a cultural tool
to relate a community’s values and ideals and is shaped and molded by these residents over time.
For example, looking at the many idioms the Chinese culture has on family, you can definitely see
how much they value that relationship. Another is with a unique Korean word “nunchi” (meaning
eye-measure) that has no English translation. This word relates to the Korean belief in gauging
how people are thinking and feeling in order to create connection, trust, and harmony.

From those samples (and perhaps some you can think from your own culture), you’ll observe that
society and language are mutually important to each other. Because every person’s linguistic
ability, knowledge, and usage are somewhat influenced by the social context of how they were
raised and taught. So, if you’re looking to learn a new language, prepare yourself to be introduced
to a new world apart from your own!
If you’re familiar with the principle of linguistic relativity, it states that the way people think of
the world is influenced directly by the language that the people use to talk about it. Or more
radically, people could only perceive aspects of the world for which their language has words.

An easier way to explain this is with color perception. The number of terms we have for the colors
we see varies from one language to another. For instance, English speakers name different shades
of blue as dark blue and light blue. Russian speakers have two distinct categories for blue: it’s

either siniy (dark blue) or goluboy (light blue). We do the same thing for another color: dark red
and light red — the latter of which we call pink! With this, people who speak two or more
languages are expected to focus differently regarding colors because different languages
distinguish color in various ways.

words.
Most people who are successful in life today were once helped by someone else. In most cases,
these people were supported by their teachers. For this reason, most of them are grateful for what
their former teachers did for them. They do not forget how their teachers helped them and
encouraged them when things were bad for them or when it seemed like there was no hope.

We have all had teachers who have impacted our lives in one way or another. We have all had
teachers who inspired us to cultivate our talents, pursue our dreams, and prepare for the future.
Some teachers can inspire students to learn more and do their best. Others can discourage students
from succeeding. That’s why it’s important for every teacher to understand that they have the
power to positively or negatively impact their students’ lives.

The same is true for many other successful people today. In almost all cases, you will find that the
people who are successful today were once helped by someone in their past – someone who cared
about them and wanted them to succeed in life.

Therefore, it is important that we teach our students not only academic knowledge but also the
values that will help them improve their lives.
Teachers can motivate students to achieve great things – both inside and outside the classroom.
Teachers who truly love their jobs are able to transfer that passion for learning to their students.

When a good teacher is excited about learning, that enthusiasm can spread like wildfire and ignite
a passion for learning in every student. This passion for knowledge can lead students to great
success throughout their lives – both personally and professionally.

ENG513_Glossary

1. Accredited :Accredited is (Of a person, organization, or course of study)
   officially recognized or authorized.
2. Allocation :The action or process of allocating or sharing out something is called
   allocation.
3. Alternative 'Concurrent' Model :A student simultaneously studies both one or
   more academic subjects, and the ways of teaching that subject, leading to a
   combined bachelor's degree and teaching credential to qualify as a teacher of that
   subject.
4. Anomaly :Something that deviates from what is standard, normal, or expected
5. Approach :It is a way of looking at teaching and learning. Underlying any
   language teaching approach is a theoretical view of what language is, and of how
   it can be learnt. An approach gives rise to methods, the way of teaching
   something, which use classroom activities or techniques to help learners learn.
6. Assess :Evaluate or judge
7. Audio Lingual Method :It is a teaching method and based on behaviorist theory,
   which postulates that certain traits of living things, and in this case humans, could
   be trained through a system of reinforcement. The correct use of a trait would
   receive positive feedback while incorrect use of that trait would receive negative
   feedback.
8. Autonomous :(Of a country or region) having the freedom to govern itself or
   control its own affairs.
9. Caution :Vigilance, carefulness
10. Collocation :The habitual juxtaposition of a particular word with another
   word or words with a frequency greater than chance is called collocation.

   which students work together to develop what aspects of a language they would
   like to learn. It is based on the Counselling-approach in which the teacher acts as
   a counselor and a paraphraser, while the learner is seen as a client and
   collaborator.

   subject matter. During the lesson students are focused on learning about
   something. This could be anything that interests them from a serious science
   subject to their favourite pop star or even a topical news story or film.
17. Contextualize :Place or study in context.
18. Continuous Professional Development :CPD is the process by which
   teachers (like other professionals) reflect upon their competencies, keep them up

ENG513
LANGUAGE: SOME THEORETICAL CONCEPTS

Defining Language Learning

Language learning refers to the process of acquiring or developing the ability to communicate in
a language, encompassing skills such as listening, speaking, reading, and writing. It may involve
the natural acquisition of a first language or the structured learning of a second language through
formal education or exposure.

Some Theoretical Concepts: Language as a System

Language as a system highlights its organized structure, consisting of rules governing phonology,
morphology, syntax, semantics, and pragmatics. This view emphasizes the interconnectedness of
linguistic components, forming the foundation for understanding and producing meaningful
communication.

Some Theoretical Concepts: Language as Discourse

Language as discourse focuses on language use in social contexts, emphasizing meaning-making
and interaction. This concept considers how spoken and written language create cohesion and
coherence, reflecting cultural norms, power dynamics, and situational appropriateness.

Some Theoretical Concepts: Language as an Ideology

Language as an ideology examines how language reflects and perpetuates societal beliefs,
identities, and power structures. This perspective reveals the role of language in shaping cultural
norms, social hierarchies, and political ideologies.

Language Teaching and Theoretical Concepts about Language

Language teaching integrates theoretical concepts to design effective methodologies. It draws on
language theories—systemic, discourse-based, or ideological—to guide instructional strategies,
curriculum design, and classroom practices, ensuring alignment with learners' needs and contexts.

A BRIEF HISTORY OF LANGUAGE TEACHING METHODS

Significance of a ‘Language Teaching Methods’ Course

A course on language teaching methods equips educators with a comprehensive understanding of
historical and modern approaches. It enables them to critically evaluate and adapt methods to meet
learners' diverse needs, fostering effective teaching practices.

Language Teaching Methods in Ancient Times

Ancient language teaching relied on rote memorization and oral repetition, often focused on
religious texts or elite communication. Teachers emphasized grammar, vocabulary, and
pronunciation without interactive or communicative approaches.

Language Teaching Methods in Europe in Early Modern Times

The Renaissance and early modern period saw the rise of grammar-translation methods,
prioritizing the study of classical languages through reading and translation. This method catered
to scholarly pursuits rather than practical communication.

Language Teaching Methods in the 19th and Early to Mid-20th Century

The Direct Method emerged in response to grammar-translation, emphasizing oral proficiency
through immersion. Later, structural and audio-lingual methods focused on repetition and drills,
grounded in behavioral psychology and structural linguistics.

Language Teaching Methods from the Mid- to Late-20th Century

The late 20th century witnessed the rise of communicative approaches, emphasizing interaction
and authentic use of language. Alternative methods like Suggestopedia, Total Physical Response,
and the Silent Way prioritized learner-centered, creative, and humanistic teaching strategies.

DIFFERENCE IN THEORY, APPROACH, METHOD, AND TECHNIQUE

What is a Theory?

A theory in language teaching provides a framework for understanding language acquisition,
offering foundational principles about how people learn and use languages.

What is an Approach?

An approach refers to the overarching philosophy or belief system guiding language instruction.
Examples include structural, communicative, or cognitive approaches.

What is a Method/Methodology?

A method or methodology outlines specific procedures or practices for teaching a language, often
derived from a broader approach. For instance, the Direct Method derives from a communicative
approach.

Types of Methods

Methods include traditional (e.g., Grammar Translation), structural (e.g., Audio-Lingual),
communicative (e.g., CLT), and humanistic approaches (e.g., Total Physical Response).

Some other terms: System, Procedure, Technique

   •   System: The organized structure of a language or teaching framework.
   •   Procedure: The steps taken to implement a method in the classroom.
   •   Technique: Specific activities or tasks that support learning objectives.

STATUS AND CONTEXT OF ENGLISH IN PAKISTAN

Status of English in Pakistan

English holds a dual status in Pakistan as both an official language and a medium of instruction. It
is associated with social mobility, economic opportunity, and international communication.

English Language and Education in Pakistan

English is integral to Pakistan's education system, often used in higher education and private
schools. However, disparities in access create challenges for equitable language proficiency.

Teaching and Learning of English in Pakistan

English teaching in Pakistan faces challenges such as untrained teachers, outdated materials, and
a lack of communicative practices. Despite this, English remains a priority for students seeking
professional advancement.

English Language Curriculum in Pakistan

The curriculum focuses on reading, writing, and grammar but often neglects communicative skills.
Reforms emphasize integrating interactive and task-based learning methods.

LTM and Constraints in Pakistan

Language teaching methods in Pakistan face constraints such as overcrowded classrooms, limited
resources, and sociopolitical factors, hindering effective implementation of modern
methodologies.

Q. Human language well-crafted and well organized comments (Topic #02)
We all know that human language is a well-organized and well-crafted instrument. That is to say, all the
basic components of a language work in tandem in a coherent and systematic manner. They are certainly
not a random collection of disparate units. From one perspective, a study of language is basically a study
of its systems and subsystems. By treating language as a system, we are merely acknowledging that each
unit of language, from a single sound to a complex word to a large text—spoken or written—has a character
of its own, and each is, in some principled way, delimited by and dependent upon its co-occurring units. As
we learn from any introductory textbook in linguistics, the core of language as a system consists of the
phonological system that deals with the patterns of sound, the semantic system that deals with the meaning
of words, and the syntactic system that deals with the rules of grammar.
Q. "Study of language is a study of its systems and subsystems. Elaborate. 5 (Topic #02)
Language as a system enables the language user to combine phonemes to form words, words to form
phrases, phrases to form sentences, and sentences to form spoken or written texts—each unit following its
own rules as well as the rules for combination. Crucial to understanding language, then, is the idea of
systematicity. Language as a system, however, is much more complex than the description. A true
understanding of the complexity of language requires a robust method of analysis. Using this “prewired”
system, children are able to distill and develop the complex grammatical system out of the speech of their
parents and caretakers. The system that the child is born with is common to the grammars of all human
languages, and hence Chomsky calls it “Universal Grammar.”
Q. Define any two meta-functions of language purposed by Halliday (Topic #3)
    1. The ideational function represents the individual’s meaning potential and relates to the expression
       and experience of the concepts, processes, and objects governing the physical and natural
       phenomena of the world around.
    2. The interpersonal function deals with the individual’s personal relationships with people.
    3. The textual function refers to the linguistic realizations of the ideational and interpersonal functions
       enabling the individual to construct coherent texts, spoken or written.
Q. Halliday prefer culture learning to mind learning define (Topic #3)
For Halliday, language communication is the product or the result of the process of interplay between the
ideational, interpersonal, and textual functions of language. Through this interplay, the meaning potential
of language is realized. Learning a language then entails learning to mean. As the child interacts with
language and language users, he or she begins to understand the meaning potential within the language, and
develops a capacity to use it. It is only through meaningful interactive activities in communicative contexts
that a learner broadens and deepens the capacity for language use. And, language use is always embedded
in a sociocultural milieu. That is why Halliday (1973) preferred to define meaning potential not in terms of
the mind but in terms of the culture.”
Q. Hymes (1972) identified these factors, and has used an acronym SPEAKING to describe them.
(Topic #3)
        Setting refers to the place and time in which the communicative event takes place.
        Participants refer to speakers and hearers and their role/relationships.
        Ends refer to the stated or unstated objectives the participants wish to accomplish.
        Act sequence refers to the form, content, and sequence of utterances.

                                      Mid-Term (Solved)

        Key refers to the manner and tone (serious, sarcastic, etc.) of the utterances.
Q. Three components of Austin's speech act theory (Topic #3)
    1. In performing a locutionary act, one often performs such an act as ―asking or answering a question,
       giving some information or an assurance or a warning, announcing a verdict or an intention,
       pronouncing sentence, making an appointment or an appeal or a criticism, making identification or
       giving a description, and the numerous like.
    2. The perlocutionary act is the effect or the consequence of an utterance in a given situation.
    3. For it to have what Austin calls illocutionary force, a speech act has to meet certain socially agreed
       upon demands or conventions. For instance, a statement like I now pronounce you man and wife
       has its intended illocutionary force only if it is uttered in a proper context (e.g., a church) and by a
       proper person (e.g., a priest). The same statement uttered by a clerk in a department store will not
       render two customers a married couple!
The statement gains its illocutionary force only because of the situational context in which it is uttered.

Neurolinguistic Programming (NLP) refers to a training philosophy and a set of training
techniques first developed by John Grindler and Richard Bandler in the mid1970s as an
alternative form of therapy.

building rapport with clients, gathering information about their internal and external views of the
world, and helping them achieve goals and bring about personal change. They sought to fill what
they perceived to be a gap in psychological thinking and practice of the early 1970s by
developing a series of step-by-step procedures that would enable people to improve themselves.

Q. Human language well crafted and well organized comments (Topic #02)

We all know that human language is a well-organized and well-crafted instrument. That is to say,
all the basic components of a language work in tandem in a coherent and systematic manner.
They are certainly not a random collection of disparate units. From one perspective, a study of
language is basically a study of its systems and subsystems. By treating language as a system, we
are merely acknowledging that each unit of language, from a single sound to a complex word to
a large text—spoken or written—has a character of its own, and each is, in some principled way,
delimited by and dependent upon its co-occurring units. As we learn from any introductory
textbook in linguistics, the core of language as a system consists of the phonological system that
deals with the patterns of sound, the semantic system that deals with the meaning of words, and
the syntactic system that deals with the rules of grammar.

Q. "Study of language is a study of its systems and subsystems. Elaborate. 5 (Topic #02)

Language as a system enables the language user to combine phonemes to form words, words to
form phrases, phrases to form sentences, and sentences to form spoken or written texts—each
unit following its own rules as well as the rules for combination. Crucial to understanding
language, then, is the idea of systematicity. Language as a system, however, is much more
complex than the description. A true understanding of the complexity of language requires a
robust method of analysis.

Using this “prewired” system, children are able to distill and develop the complex grammatical
system out of the speech of their parents and caretakers. The system that the child is born with is
common to the grammars of all human languages, and hence Chomsky calls it “Universal
Grammar.”

For Halliday, language communication is the product or the result of the process of interplay
between the ideational, interpersonal, and textual functions of language. Through this interplay,
the meaning potential of language is realized. Learning a language then entails learning to mean.

meaning potential within the language, and develops a capacity to use it. It is only through
meaningful interactive activities in communicative contexts that a learner broadens and deepens
the capacity for language use. And, language use is always embedded in a sociocultural milieu.
That is why Halliday (1973) preferred to define meaning potential not in terms of the mind but in
terms of the culture.”

Q. Human language well crafted and well organized comments (Topic #02)

We all know that human language is a well-organized and well-crafted instrument. That is to say,
all the basic components of a language work in tandem in a coherent and systematic manner.
They are certainly not a random collection of disparate units. From one perspective, a study of
language is basically a study of its systems and subsystems. By treating language as a system, we
are merely acknowledging that each unit of language, from a single sound to a complex word to
a large text—spoken or written—has a character of its own, and each is, in some principled way,
delimited by and dependent upon its co-occurring units. As we learn from any introductory
textbook in linguistics, the core of language as a system consists of the phonological system that
deals with the patterns of sound, the semantic system that deals with the meaning of words, and
the syntactic system that deals with the rules of grammar.

Q. "Study of language is a study of its systems and subsystems. Elaborate. 5 (Topic #02)

Language as a system enables the language user to combine phonemes to form words, words to
form phrases, phrases to form sentences, and sentences to form spoken or written texts—each
unit following its own rules as well as the rules for combination. Crucial to understanding
language, then, is the idea of systematicity. Language as a system, however, is much more
complex than the description. A true understanding of the complexity of language requires a
robust method of analysis.

Using this “prewired” system, children are able to distill and develop the complex grammatical
system out of the speech of their parents and caretakers. The system that the child is born with is
common to the grammars of all human languages, and hence Chomsky calls it “Universal
Grammar.”

Q. Define any two meta-functions of language purposed by Halliday (Topic #3)

   1. The ideational function represents the individual’s meaning potential and relates to the
      expression and experience of the concepts, processes, and objects governing the physical
      and natural phenomena of the world around.
   2. The interpersonal function deals with the individual’s personal relationships with people.
   3. The textual function refers to the linguistic realizations of the ideational and interpersonal
      functions enabling the individual to construct coherent texts, spoken or written.

Q. Halliday prefer culture learning to mind learning define (Topic #3)

For Halliday, language communication is the product or the result of the process of interplay
between the ideational, interpersonal, and textual functions of language. Through this interplay,
the meaning potential of language is realized. Learning a language then entails learning to mean.
As the child interacts with language and language users, he or she begins to understand the
meaning potential within the language, and develops a capacity to use it. It is only through
meaningful interactive activities in communicative contexts that a learner broadens and deepens
the capacity for language use. And, language use is always embedded in a sociocultural milieu.
That is why Halliday (1973) preferred to define meaning potential not in terms of the mind but in
terms of the culture.”

Q. Hymes (1972) identified these factors, and has used an acronym SPEAKING to describe
them. (Topic #3)

        Setting refers to the place and time in which the communicative event takes place.
        Participants refer to speakers and hearers and their role/relationships.
        Ends refer to the stated or unstated objectives the participants wish to accomplish.

      It is profitable to think of language ideologies as a cluster of concepts consisting of converging dimensions:

               the interests of a specific social or cultural group”

               meaningful social divisions
           • Third, “members may display varying degrees of awareness of local language ideologies”

The poverty of stimulus by Chomsky

The language input exposed to the child is both quantitatively and qualitatively poor but still the child is able to
produce, in a short period of time, language output that is immensely rich.

Universal Grammar - a set of abstract concepts governing the grammatical structure of all languages that are
genetically encoded in the human brain. It comprises:

       the individual to construct coherent texts, spoken or written.

ideational, interpersonal, and textual functions of language.

       • Setting refers to the place and time in which the communicative event takes place.
       • Participants refer to speakers and hearers and their role/relationships.
       • Ends refer to the stated or unstated objectives the participants wish to accomplish.
       • Act sequence refers to the form, content, and sequence of utterances.

    2) Sometimes as an individualized group of statements - relates to specific formations or fields
    3) Sometimes as a regulated practice that accounts for a number of statements - relates to sociopolitical
       structures

Text

A text means what it means. In other words, texts are political because all discursive formations are political.

travelers, politicians and administrators, that shape and structure Western representations of colonized people.

When a teacher believes in language as a certain kind of entity, it affects his or her way of thinking about language

Q: What is CONTENT-BASED INSTRUCTION?
       Content-Based Instruction (CBI) refers to an approach to second language teaching in which teaching is
organized around the content or information that students will acquire, rather than around a linguistic or other type
of syllabus. Krahnke offers the following definition:
       It is the teaching of content or information in the language being learned with little or no direct or explicit
effort to teach the language separately from the content being taught. (Krahnke, 1987, p. 65).

Q Define the term ‘content’ used in content based instruction.
    The term content has become a popular one both within language teaching and in the popular media. New
York Times columnist and linguistic pundit William Safire addressed it in one of his columns in 1998 and noted:
    If any word in the English language is hot and buzz-worthy, surpassing even millennium in both general
discourse and insiders, that word is content. (New York Times, August 19, 1998, 15) Although content is used
with a variety of different meanings in language teaching, it most frequently refers to the substance or subject
matter that we learn or communicate through language rather than the language used to convey it.

Q: Write down few programs based on content study.
    Other educational initiatives since the late 1970s that also emphasize the principle of acquiring content
through language rather than the study of language for its own sake include Language across the Curriculum,
Immersion Education, Immigrant On-Arrival Programs, Programs for Students with Limited English Proficiency,
and Language for Specific Purposes.
Q: What is the role of Content in other Curriculum Designs and Content-Based Instruction?
    Language skills should also be taught in the content subjects and not left exclusively for the English teacher to
deal with. This report influenced American education as well, and the slogan "Every teacher, an English teacher"
became familiar. Like other cross-disciplinary proposals, this one never had the classroom impact that its
advocates had hoped for. Nevertheless, subject-matter texts appeared that included exercises dealing with
language practice, and the need for collaboration between subject- matter teachers and language teachers was
emphasized. In some cases, curricular material was produced that integrated subject matter and language teaching
goals, such as the Singaporean Primary Pilot Project in the 1970s classroom texts integrating science, math, and
language study. Immersion Education has also had a strong influence on the theory of Content-Based Instruction.
Q What is Immersion Education? Write a short not on it.
    Immersion Education is a type of foreign language instruction in which the regular school curriculum is taught
through the medium of the foreign language. The foreign language is the vehicle for content instruction; it is not
the subject of instruction. Thus, for example, an English-speaking child might enter a primary school in which the
medium of instruction for all the content subjects is French.
Q What are the goals of an immersion program?
    Student goals of an immersion program include:
(1) Developing a high level of proficiency in the foreign language;
(2) Developing positive attitudes toward those who speak the foreign language & toward their culture(s);
(3) Developing English language skills commensurate with expectations for a student's age and abilities;
(4) Gaining designated skills and knowledge in the content areas of the curriculum.

Q: Write few lines on Immigrant On-Arrival Programs.
    Immigrant On-Arrival Programs typically focus on the newly arrived immigrants in a country and their need
for survival. Such learners typically need to learn how to deal with differing kinds of real-world content as a basis
for social survival. Design of such courses in Australia was among the first attempts to integrate notional,
functional, grammatical, and lexical specifications built around particular themes and situations. A typical course
would cover language needed to deal with immigration bureaucracies, finding accommodations, shopping, finding
a job, and so forth. The methodology of the Australian on-arrival courses was based on the Direct Method

situations. In current on-arrival programs, a competency-based approach is often used in which a teaching syllabus

designed to provide in-class or pullout instruction for any school-age children whose language competence is
insufficient to participate fully in normal school instruction. Early versions of such programs were largely
grammar-based.

                           ENG513_Language Teaching Methods
                                 Quiz for Final-Term

   1. It refers to the substance or subject matter that we learn or communicate through language
      rather than the language used to convey it. (Content)
   2. In current on-arrival programs, a _____ approach is often used in which a teaching syllabus
      is developed around the competencies learners are presumed to need in different survival
      situations. (Competency-based)
   3. It is a movement that seeks to serve the language needs of learners who need language in
      order to carry out specific roles. (Language for specific purposes)
   4. ‘People learn a second language more successfully when they use the language as a means
      of acquiring information, rather than as an end in itself’. (second)
   5. Content-Based Instruction is in the "_____" school of pedagogy. (learning by doing)
   6. Two early applications of a task-based approach within a communicative framework for
      language teaching were the _________ (1975) and the Bangalore Project. (Malaysian
      Communicational Syllabus)
   7. Foster and Skehan (1996) propose a _____ functional, personal, narrative, and decision
      making tasks. (three-way)
   8. These tasks have a psycho linguistic basis in SLA theory and research. (Pedagogical tasks)
   9. In this kind of task, learners engage in discussion and exchange of ideas. They do not need
      to reach agreement. (Opinion exchange tasks)
   10.Eclectic approach is the combination of _______ approaches and methodologies depending
      on the aims of the lesson and the abilities of the learners. (various)
   11.The teaching approach which is understood more than a set of very general principles that
      can be applied and interpreted in a variety of ways is __________. (Communicative
      Language Teaching)
   12.A teacher has to consider carefully the context in which teaching and learning occurs when
      applying approaches or ___________. (methods)
   13.In language teaching the _________ innovations will influence both the content and the
      form of instructional delivery. (technological)
   14.The approaches and methods used by the _______ flexibly and creatively on their own
      judgment and experience. (teachers)
   15.According to Green (1986), the language that is used at a _________ moment is the
      selected language. (certain)

   18.The concept of ________is interpreted differently in the field of SLA, psychology and
      education. (bilingualism)
   19.In which of the following approaches to writing, knowledge-transformation is an important
      implementation device. (Socio-cognitive)
   20.It means a systematic body of ideas, organized from a particular point of view. (Ideology)
   21.The __________ teaching method is commonly used in Pakistani Bilingual context.
      (Grammar Translation)

4. Language as a system enables the language user to combine _______ to form words, words to
   form phrases, phrases to form sentences, and sentences to form spoken or written texts.

8. ELT stands for ____________. (English Language Teaching)
9. In the Western world, from 17th to 19th centuries, learning of which of the following languages
   was associated with speaker’s intellectuality? (Greek and Latin)
10.Lack of __________ in the areas of language planning in education is the major problem in
   Pakistan. (research)
11.In __________, there is no usual listening or speaking practice, and very little attention is
   placed on pronunciation. (GTM)
12.In a typical Pakistani English classroom, __________ is commonly used. (GTM)

14.Direct Method was established in _____ and Germany around 1900. (France)

   Britain)
18.Which of the following is firmly entrenched in the domains of power in Pakistan since 1947?
   (English Language)
19.The practicality of English language opens innumerable prospects in the _____ and financial
   world. (social)
20.According to Warsi (1994), ELT methodology in Pakistan is not based on _____ approach.
   (need based)
21.Richards (2011) identifies the purpose of _____ for curriculum development in English
   language teaching. (needs analysis)
22.According to Abbas (1998): despite the massive inputs into teaching of English, the national
   results are abysmally _____. (poor)
23.In Pakistan, the examination system is based on _______________ skill. (writing)
24.Reading skill is given importance in _____ education system. (Pakistani)
25.GTM is more commonly used in _____ schools in Pakistan. (government)
26.English has a unique significance around the globe due to its status as a _____. (lingua franca)
27.HE stands for _________. (higher education)
